Installation of the CCTab package
To install this package first unpack it inside some GAP root directory in the subdirectory pkg (see ). Then the CCTab package can already be loaded and used. But we strongly recommend to compile a kernel function and some standalone programs as well during installation. This will speed up some computations.
The standalone programs assume that the library files and header files of the FLINT library are installed. If this is not yet the case, install them first via your operating systems package manager (package libflint-dev or similar), or directly from https://flintlib.org/.
To install the extra functions go to the directory pkg/CCTab-... or pkg/cctab/ to which the package was extracted and call
/bin/sh ./configure [path]
where [path] is a path to the main GAP root directory (if not given, the default ../.. is assumed).
Afterwards call make to compile the code.
You can run a test of the installation by typing make test.
After installation the package can be used with LoadPackage("CCTab");.
To see some progress information during longer computations the following info class can be set to a non-zero level:
This is an Info class for the CCTab-package. By SetInfoLevel(InfoCCTab, level); with level between 1 and 3 you can switch on the printing of some information during the computations of certain CCTab-functions.
The default level is 0.

The main functionality of CCTab
This package can be useful for users who want to compute ordinary character tables of given finite groups.
By loading this package the default method for is overwritten for those groups for which the &GAP; library would use .
If this is all you want, you do not need to know any further details about the functions in CCTab.
But the functions in CCTab can also be used interactively to construct character tables of groups which are not handled easily by the generic algorithm. In this case you may be interested in more details about how this package works.
There are also some functions, e.g., , or which may be of independent interest for other applications.

Utility functions from the CCTab package
This package implements various utility functions which may also be of independent interest. For example, there are functions for identifying the conjugacy class of a given element, or for computing all power maps of a finite group, or for computing information about rational conjugacy classes. Furthermore there are utilities for certain integer matrices.

Power maps and rational classes
Let x_1, \ldots, x_k be conjugacy class representatives of a finite group G. The n-th power map of G is the list of k integers such that the i-th entry is j when x_i^n is conjugate to x_j. If x_i has order m then the power map of class i is a list of length m such that the n-th entry is j if x_i^{{n-1}} is conjugate to x_j.
Let x be an element of order m in a group G. The rational class of x is the union of the conjugacy classes of all elements which generate the same cyclic subgroup of G as x (that is, of all x^i with \gcd(i, m) = 1).

Induction from elementary subgroups
To compute the irreducible characters of a finite group G we are interested in the characters of G induced from p-elementary subgroups \langle{x}\rangle \times P, where p is a prime, x \in G is of order not divisible by p, and P is a p-subgroup of the centralizer of x in G. An elementary subgroup of G is a p-elementary subgroup for some prime p. We are mainly interested in maximal elementary subgroups (those not contained in larger elementary subgroups).

Some utilities for integer matrices
This package uses a variant of the LLL algorithm to find the irreducible characters from another integral basis of the lattice of generalized characters. And there are functions to compute Hermite normal forms and inverses of unimodular matrices.
There are variants of these functions written in &GAP;. But we also provide variants which use standalone programs which need to be compiled during installation. These depend on the FLINT library, see . These standalone programs use several threads. The number of these threads is configured in the variable NRFlintThreads, it defaults to 8 (but you can change it, depending on the number of cores of your machine).
